Load on board: 짐을 자동차에 싣다 (M13's 짐, M50's 자동차). ㄷ-irregular — the family of 듣다 (M2), 걷다 (M6), and 묻다 (M28) gains a fourth member: ㄷ softens to ㄹ before vowels — 실어요, 실었어요. Second job in publishing: 신문에 기사를 싣다 (M8, M48's 기사) — pages carry articles the way trucks carry boxes.

en: to pile up, stack; to build up
notes: Stack it with intent — walls, boxes, snow forts — but Korea keeps its real ledger in the abstract column: 경험을 쌓다 (M33) = build up experience, 실력을 쌓다 — M44 glossed M26's 실력 as 'built skill', and this is the verb that does the building. Careers, trust, and mileage points are all 쌓다-ed one layer at a time. Says 싸타.

쌓다 through M36's passive 이: it piles up on its own, nobody stacking. 눈이 쌓이다 (M11's snow) is the pretty version; 스트레스가 쌓이다 (M14) is the one Korea actually says daily. M53 filed the relief half of the cycle — 피로가 풀리다, M36's 풀리다 untying fatigue; here is the debit side that fills the account first. The badge form 쌓인 (M24) fronts every tired sentence.

en: to yell, let out (a scream); to splurge
notes: 소리를 지르다 (M19) = let out a yell — where M51's 소리치다 launches words at someone, 지르다 launches pure volume: roller coasters, goals, cockroaches. 르-family (M7): 질러요, 질렀어요. Modern wallet slang runs on it too: 질렀다 = I splurged — the shopping cart, screamed at.

Contact, barely made: 손이 닿다 (M8) = within reach — 손이 안 닿는 곳 is where every itch lives, and where stores shelve the expensive things. Hearts make the same contact: 마음이 닿다 (M19) = the feeling got through. Radar: one stroke from M13's 닫다 (close) — 닿다 touches, 닫다 shuts.

en: to reach, extend to; to go crazy
notes: Two dictionary entries, one spelling, both essential. Sense one, reach: 영향을 미치다 (影響 = influence, frozen) is how news-Korean says 'affects', and 생각이 거기까지 미치지 못했어요 = my thinking didn't reach that far. Sense two, mad: 미쳤어? = are you crazy?! — drama-frequent, friends-only; aimed at a stranger it is a genuine insult, so keep it inside 반말 range. Slang has flipped it into praise: 미친 맛 (M18) = insanely good.

A double agent split by hanja. 取 take, in full formal dress: 휴식을 취하다 (休息 = rest, frozen) — the way announcements and doctors say 'get some rest.' 醉 drunk: 술에 취하다 (M9) — 취했어요? = are you drunk? The drunk sense wanders licenseless: 분위기에 취하다 (M26) = drunk on the atmosphere, no bottle required.

en: to exhaust, give one's all; to fulfill
notes: M39's 최선 note already did the arithmetic — '최선을 다하다 = give it everything (다 + 하다: to do-it-all, M9's 다 finally verbing)' — and today the verb stands on its own card: use up completely, carry out fully. 힘을 다해서 (M14) = with everything one has; 책임을 다하다 (M39's 책임) = discharge a duty to the last item. Effort, patience, and phone batteries all eventually 다했다.

屬 belong-속: ~에 속하다 files a thing into its drawer — the taxonomy verb of textbooks and quiz shows. 한국은 아시아에 속해요 (M31's 아시아); 수박은 과일에 속할까요? (M30, M3) — the eternal picnic debate, officially yes. Radar, third 속: M28's 속 is the native deep-inside, 약속's (M5) 속 is bind-束, and this one is membership-屬.

提供 hold-forth-supply: provide, in the register of hotels and terms-of-service. 호텔이 아침 식사를 제공해요 (M23, M3's 식사); 정보를 제공하다 (M33) is the phrasing of every app permission screen you've ever skimmed. M9's 주다 gives person-to-person; 제공하다 supplies — officially, with a logo on it.

考慮 examine-ponder: consider, weigh — the boardroom's thinking verb. 고려해 보겠습니다 (M16's try-machine wearing M49's -겠-) = we will take it into consideration — Korea's politest no; do not hold your breath. Radar: a perfect homophone of 高麗 Goryeo, the dynasty that gave 'Korea' its name — context keeps the kingdom and the committee apart.

M32's 느끼다 through M35's -아/어지다: the feeling arrives on its own, no feeler required. 가을이 느껴져요 (M11) = you can feel autumn in the air; 진심이 느껴졌어요 (M24's 진심) = the sincerity came through. M34's 느낌 is the noun this verb delivers to your door.

M1's 없다 through M35's become-machine: come to not-be-there. 지갑이 없어졌어요 (M21) = my wallet's gone — said at the worst possible moment. Pain, stains, and snack supplies all 없어지다. M35's 사라지다 vanishes with some mystery to it; 없어지다 just stops being where you left it.

M3's 만들다, done unto by M35's machine: be made. 치즈는 우유로 만들어져요 (M40's 치즈, M2's 우유) — (으)로 marks the raw material. Laws, friendships, and new words are all 만들어지다-ed too: the passive voice of the national verb for making.

M1's 크다 + M35's -아/어지다: get bigger — the become-machine's textbook example, finally enrolled. 소리가 점점 커져요 (M19); problems escalate the same way: 문제가 커졌어요 (M7) = this got big. Radar: one vowel from M36's 켜지다 (turn on by itself) — 커지다 grows, 켜지다 lights up.

en: to break out, unfold (events); to widen
notes: The happen-verb of headlines: events break out and unfold on their own — 큰 사건이 벌어졌어요 (M36's 사건). Radar for M56's 벌이다 file (which already tracks 벌다 and 버리다): you 벌이다 the affair; left alone, it 벌어지다-s — launcher and launched. Second sense, gaps: 사이가 벌어지다 (M6's 사이) = a relationship drifts apart — seams, teeth, and friendships all widen with it.

M40's 담다 through M36's passive 기: be held inside. M40 reported that letters, gifts, and songs all claim to be 마음을 담아서 made — 담기다 is how the claim gets inspected: 마음이 담긴 선물 (M19, M9) = a gift with heart actually in it. Bowls do the literal version: 그릇에 담긴 반찬 (M18, M3).

M19's 부르다 through M36's passive 리: be called. The naming frame runs on M32's quote-라고: X라고 불려요 = is called X — how nicknames, titles, and legends get pinned on. Radar: an unrelated 불리다 soaks things — 콩을 불리다 (M40's 콩) = soak the beans overnight; the particle tells you which one showed up.

M56's 발견하다 note promised 'the passive rides free on the 되다-machine (M36): 발견되다' — receipt, paid. Swap the 하다 and the discovery happens TO the thing: 새로운 사실이 발견됐어요 (M35's 새롭다, M24's 사실). The register of museums, headlines, and detective-show epilogues.

進行 advance-go (the parent 진행하다 = to conduct, frozen here): be under way. 회의가 진행되고 있어요 (M10) — meetings, ceremonies, and roadworks are all 진행 중, the sign-language the 사용 중 S2 taught you to read. the swap-the-하다 machine (M36) in its natural habitat: the official announcement.

M10's 사용하다, flipped by the 되다-swap (M36): be used. 이 단어는 요즘 잘 사용되지 않아요 (M10's 단어, M26's 요즘) — the dictionary's polite way of saying 'dated.' You've read 사용 중 on doors since M10; now you can conjugate the other side of the sign.

en: to be thought, be considered (to be)
notes: M10's 생각하다 gone formal-passive: be thought, seem — written Korean holding an opinion at arm's length. ~(으)로 생각됩니다 = it is thought that — the news anchor's shrug, the report's hedge. In speech you'd reach for the 것 같다 hedge (M34); on paper, 생각되다 wears the tie.

M56's 관련 (gate-link) verbed by the 되다-machine: be related to. The working form wears M24's badge: ~와 관련된 = related to ~ — 시험과 관련된 정보 (M10, M33) fronts half the internet's search results. M56 handed you 관련 기사 ready-stacked; now the badge builds itself from any noun you like.

The strong very that specializes in feelings: 무척 보고 싶었어요 = I missed you terribly, 무척 그리웠어요 (M42's 그립다, at full strength). M11 handed you 아주 (neutral), 너무 (excess turned 'so'), and 진짜/정말 (really); 무척 sits a rung above them all, with a faint smell of ink — the diary's very. Its suffering twin is next.

무척 feels; 몹시 suffers: 몹시 아팠어요 (M14's 아프다, at its worst), 몹시 추운 겨울 — pain, fevers, and brutal weather are its beat. Both of these strongs are print-flavored; out loud, Korean mostly reaches for M11's 너무 and 진짜 and saves 무척/몹시 for when it writes things down.

M11's 너무 wearing an emphatic tail: 너무나 아름다운 밤 (M22's 아름답다, wearing M24's badge) = a night SO very beautiful. This is the register of song lyrics and drama finales — one notch more swept-away than plain 너무. When Korean wants to sigh in print, it adds the 나.

The understatement professional: 꽤 괜찮아요 = quite decent (M7's 괜찮다, upgraded by restraint), 꽤 멀어요 = farther than you'd hoped. It grades one honest notch below 아주 — praise with its eyebrows kept level, which from a reserved reviewer is praise indeed. One syllable, spelled with the rare ㅙ.

The measuring not-that: with a negative it sets the size — 그리 멀지 않아요 = not THAT far. M17's 별로 already taught the shrug ('The politest possible shrug,' says its note); 그리 is drier — 별로 shrugs, 그리 measures. It's M33's 그렇게 ('that much') in one syllable, and period dramas still use it for thither: 그리 오너라 — partner of the archaic 이리 오너라 that M55's 이리 note bellows. Radar: no kin to 그리고 (M7), 그리다 (M15), or 그립다 (M42).

Two jobs, one wheeze. Barely-made-it: 겨우 도착했어요 (M8's verb, out of breath) = only just got there. And belittling-small: 겨우 십 분 = a mere ten minutes, 겨우 그거? = THAT's all? Either way it measures the gap between effort and result and finds it embarrassing.

但只 but-only: 단지 농담이었어요 = it was merely a joke (M19's 농담, hastily walked back). The dressed-up cousin of M55's 단 — the single-單 hiding in 단어, per that note; 단 clips a quantity, 단지 deflates a whole clause. Radar: the apartment-complex 단지 (團地 — 아파트 단지, the block-forest of Korean housing) is a different word wearing the same syllables.

M7's 적다 (few) run through M39's even-if machine: even-at-its-fewest = at least — the negotiator's floor. 적어도 세 번 = at least three times; 적어도 저는 안 했어요 = well, at least I didn't. A concession with a spine: it gives ground and then names the line it won't cross.

No aim, no brakes: 마구 먹었어요 = ate like the fridge owed you money, 마구 샀어요 = shopped with the cart, not the list. Its clipped street form is one entry down — and M26's 막걸리 wears that clip on its label: the roughly-strained folk rice wine, by its usual reading. This 마구, moonlighting at the brewery.

One syllable, two dictionary rows, both essential. Row one, just-now: 막 도착했어요 = arrived this second — shoulder to shoulder with M38's 방금 (which 'points backward only'; 막 hugs the verb even tighter). Row two, 마구 pressed flat: 과자를 막 먹어요 = shoveling them in — the dictionary itself glosses this 막 as 마구. Context sorts them: next to an arrival it's timing, next to a mess it's manner. And M12's 막차 note ('막 (last) + 차') holds a third 막 — the last-one prefix. One sound, three careers.

The boundary-setter, almost always negated: 함부로 말하지 마세요 = watch your mouth (the don't-machine from M14, drawing the line), 함부로 만지지 마세요 = hands off (M41's 만지다) — museum signs, hospital wards, and wounded feelings all post it. To do a thing 함부로 is to do it as if nobody and nothing deserved care.

M4's 모르다 in a trench coat: doing it so someone STAYS not-knowing — 몰래 나갔어요 = slipped out (M8's 나가다, on tiptoe), and 엄마 몰래 = behind mom's back — the owner of the ignorance parks right in front. Surprise parties, midnight snacks, and every drama's second act run on it.

몰래's misdemeanor cousin: low stakes, soft footsteps — 문을 살짝 열었어요 = opened the door a crack (M13's 열다, being considerate). Also physically slight: 살짝 매워요 = just a touch spicy (M3's 맵다, dialed down). Where M9's 조금 measures, 살짝 tiptoes.

The startle-shape: 깜짝 놀랐어요 — M26's 놀라다 note staged this exact scene ('깜짝 is the jump itself'), and today the jump gets its own card. 깜짝 파티 = the surprise party (M19's 파티, ambushed). The flinch, painted as a word — the gap deck holds the yelp it produces.

Brimful — a container meeting its limit: 물이 가득 = water to the top, 한 잔 가득 (M5's counter, generously read). The frequency list files it with its verb, 가득 차다 (to be full) — the same 차다 that M37's 채우다 note decoded inside make-full — so with 채우다 you do it yourself: 가득 채웠어요. Buses, hearts, and parking lots all take it.

The armful adverb: 잔뜩 샀어요 = bought a haul, 잔뜩 먹었어요 = ate to capacity. Skies use it too: 구름이 잔뜩 낀 하늘 (M11's 구름) = packed with cloud — that cloud-verb 끼다 sounds like M21's ring-wearing 끼다, but the dictionaries file them apart. Calibration: 가득 fills a container; 잔뜩 loads a person, a sky, a mood.

M55's 온 (whole — 'stamped on the front of a noun,' says its note) welded to the container-통 that M44's 필통 note indexed (물통, 쓰레기통): the whole container of a scene — 세상이 온통 하얘요 = the world is white to every edge (M22's 세상, M49's 하얗다). Where M9's 다 counts everything, 온통 paints everything.

M9's 조금 + M43's 씩, fully decodable — and already folklore: M43's sentence deck ordered 조금씩 저축하세요, and its gap deck filed the mountain that method builds (티끌 모아 태산). The encouragement adverb: 조금씩 좋아지고 있어요 = it's getting better, a little at a time. Say it about your Korean; it will be true.

en: just in time, as luck would have it
notes: Lucky timing: 마침 잘 왔어요 = you came at the perfect moment — the thing needed and the thing arriving in the same minute. Radar against M35's 마침내: 마침 is the coincidence, 마침내 the long-awaited release ('keep 마침내 for prose and gravity,' per its note). 마침 involves no waiting at all — just the universe briefly cooperating.

The adverb of things that never happened: 끝내 오지 않았어요 = in the end, they never came — it usually rides a negative, closing a long wait with a slow shake of the head. Family of M8's 끝나다 and M16's 끝내다, frozen mid-stride. Wink: the slang verb 끝내주다 ('it finishes you off' = it's incredible) wears the same stem in a far better mood.

M26's 이제 with a bent vowel — the same hinge between chapters ('now-as-opposed-to-before,' per that note), warmer diction: 인제 왔어? = oh, NOW you show up. Standard dictionaries list it, but it carries the flavor S4's 사투리 tour taught you to hear — grandmother's kitchen, not the news desk. Like 이제, it also moonlights as a noun: 인제부터 = from now on.

漸次 gradual-sequence: M35's 점점 in a suit. Same creep, different podium — the report writes 점차 where the friend says 점점, and both love M35's -아/어지다, the becoming-machine whose pace they measure: 점차 좋아져요 reads like a briefing; 점점 좋아져요 sounds like a text.

The -히 rack's generalizer: 흔히 볼 수 있는 새 = a bird you can see anywhere — M10's can-machine wearing M24's badge. Calibration: M8's 자주 counts YOUR repetitions; 흔히 states the world's — what is typical, not what is habitual. Newspaper sentences lean on it the way conversations lean on 자주.

M6's 멀다 through the adverb press: far as a direction of doing — 멀리 갔어요 = went far away, 멀리서 왔어요 = came from afar. And the life advice: 멀리 보세요 = look far ahead — Korean files long-term thinking as good eyesight.

M6's 가깝다 through the same press — the ㅂ softens out, exactly as its note's 가까워요 warned: 가까이 오세요 = come closer. The list grants it a second calling as a noun: 역 가까이에 살아요 = I live in the station's near. 멀리/가까이 — one press, two directions; the space pair complete.

M22's 깊다, twice over. The adverb: 깊이 생각해 보세요 = think it over deeply (M10's 생각하다 through M16's try-machine). And the noun — depth — which slots straight into M57's ruler rack beside 길이 and 높이. Same spelling, two grammar jobs; Korean lets 깊이 keep both, and so does the exam.

Apart on purpose: 따로 살아요 = we live separately, 따로 주문했어요 (M3's verb) = ordered separately. Doubled at the register — 따로따로 계산해 주세요 (M9's 계산하다) = separate checks, please. Kin of M55's 딴, the street's 다른; and the gap deck holds the philosophy it builds with M29's 또: 따로 또 같이.

M34's 분명하다 promised this exact adverb — '분명히 봤어요 = I DEFINITELY saw it' — and today it clocks in: the eyewitness word, sworn to what your own eyes hold. 분명히 말했는데 = I clearly SAID so (and yet…). The -히 rack's courtroom member; its note-sibling 확실히 (M42) checks the facts, 분명히 trusts the eyes.

M11's 정말 with the -로 tail — the sworn-testimony upgrade: 정말로 몰랐어요 = I truly did not know. That tail has been quietly shipping for ages: 바로 (M28), 서로 (M24), 새로 (M35), 스스로 (M56), 별로 (M17) — an adverb-maker hiding in plain sight, and today it signs three more.

M39's 절대 note already spelled it '절대(로)' — today the parenthesis opens. Same law: a negative must follow — 절대로 안 돼요, 절대로 잊지 않을 거예요 (M15's 잊다, defied at full length). The 로 adds a fist on the table; the grammar underneath doesn't move.

M24's 똑같다 through the -이 press — 같이 itself (M9) came off this line first: 똑같이 나눠 주세요 = split it exactly evenly (M56's 나누다, under supervision). Kids watch the cake cut with this word loaded; copy the teacher 똑같이 and the dance class goes fine.

The standout adverb: 유난히 춥네요 = it's UNUSUALLY cold — weather smalltalk upgraded with a statistic you made up on the spot. From 유난 (a fuss, a standing-out: 유난을 떨다 = make a big production of it); with -히 it marks the one that broke the pattern.

M39's 충분하다 (充分 filled-portion) on adverb duty: 충분히 쉬세요 = rest plenty (M8's 쉬다, doctor's orders), 충분히 생각했어요 = I've thought it through enough. The -히 rack's generous member — it certifies the portion was met.

The piling connective: sentence one states the trouble, 게다가 stacks more on — 게다가 비까지 왔어요 = and on TOP of that, it rained (까지 doing its 'even' job). It reads as 거기에다가 — 'onto there' — pressed flat. Register: M56's 또한 you 'say aloud only from a podium'; 게다가 is how the complaint actually sounds at the table.

게다가's twin with slightly older manners, built on M9's 더 (more): 더구나 혼자였어요 = and what's more, they were alone. It tilts a notch more written than 게다가 and a notch more spoken than M56's 또한 — the middle rung of the piling ladder, favored by narrators.

M10's 잘 note has taught the spaced 잘 못 해요 (can't do it WELL) since Ring 1 — close the space and blame arrives: 잘못 = a fault. 제 잘못이에요 (M17's 제) = it's my fault, the apology's load-bearing sentence. Fused, it also adverbs as 'wrongly': 잘못 들었어요 (M2's 듣다) = I misheard; 전화를 잘못 걸었어요 (M20's 걸다) = wrong number. Spacing radar: 잘 못 해요 pleads inability; 잘못했어요 admits guilt.

en: to do wrong, be at fault
notes: 잘못, verbed: to do wrong. 잘못했어요 = I was in the wrong — one rung below M4's 미안해요 and 죄송합니다: those regret, this one ADMITS. Radar: M17's 잘하다/못하다 grade skill — 노래를 못해요 earns sympathy, 잘못했어요 asks forgiveness. Kids deliver it with both hands raised; adults deliver it when regret alone won't cover the bill.

en: to go well, turn out well
notes: M10's 잘 + M10's 되다, fused into one verb: to go well — 잘되고 있어요 = it's coming along. The blessing built on it is national currency: 다 잘될 거예요 = it'll all work out (the future -(으)ㄹ 거예요, M8) — handed to every worried friend, exam-taker, and job-seeker. Its shadow twin is next on the shelf.

en: to go wrong, turn out badly
notes: To go WRONG: 주소가 잘못됐어요 (M12's 주소) = the address is wrong; 어디가 잘못됐어요? = where did it go wrong? And the euphemism every drama leans on: 잘못되면 (the -(으)면 condition, M20) = 'if something should happen (to someone)' — Korean's gentlest way to name the worst case without naming it.

失手 lose-your-hands — M35's 실패하다 note filed the family: 실수 (M16, lose-your-hands), 실례 (M33, lose-courtesy), 실패 (lose-the-attempt). Today the first one's noun stands alone, completing what M16's 실수하다 started. Radar vs 잘못: a 실수 slips, a 잘못 offends — one gets a laugh, the other gets an apology. The sentence deck runs the calibration.

Morally, logically right: 옳은 말이에요 (M4's 말) = that's a true word. Says 올타 — and 옳은 says 오른, exactly M6's 오른쪽, no accident: in Korean as in English, the right hand has long been the 'right' one. Radar vs M15's 맞다: 맞다 checks answers (맞아요!, the quiz bell); 옳다 judges choices — an answer can be 맞다, only a decision can be 옳다.

en: to be upright, proper; to apply, spread on
notes: One spelling, two NIKL headwords, both yours today. Upright: 바른 자세 (posture — riding frozen) at the desk, 바른 말 (M4's 말) from the mouth — correctness as good posture. And spread-on, a full transitive verb: 상처에 약을 바르다 — M10's 약 onto M36's 상처 — plus sunscreen, jam, and wallpaper. Both run the 르-family table (M7): 발라요. Straighten it or smear it.

正確 correct-solid: 정답's 正 (M44 — the one hiding inside 정말 since M11) + the firm-確 of 확인하다 (M20). 정확한 시간 (M1's 시간) = the exact time; 정확하게 = precisely (the -게 adverb, M33). The watchmaker's adjective: where M15's 맞다 merely isn't wrong, 정확하다 is on the money.

en: to be fitting, suitable, just right
notes: M15's 맞다 with 알 in front: fitting, just-right — 알맞은 크기 (M57's 크기) = the right size, 알맞은 양 = the right amount (this shelf supplies both rulers). Textbook Korean runs on it: 알맞은 답을 고르세요 = choose the fitting answer — the instruction printed above half the exercises you will ever solve.

틀리다 (M15) through the -ㅁ factory (M33), plus 없다 (M1): no-miss-exists = certain. 틀림없어요 = no doubt about it; 틀림없이 = without fail — the same -이 adverb that built 없이 (M32). The detective's adjective: certainty phrased as the absence of error.

簡單: a slip-簡 (frozen — the bamboo slats writing once lived on) + the single-單 of M55's 단, the one hiding in 단어, this app's own name. Simple as in SHORT: 간단한 질문 (M10's 질문), 간단한 답 (M15's 답) — over in a minute. 간단하게 말하면 (M4's 말하다, the -게 adverb M33) = to put it briefly.

單純 single-pure — M55's 單 again, plus a pure-純 (frozen). The precision pair: 간단하다 measures length (a 간단한 답 is short); 단순하다 measures complexity (a 단순한 문제 has one moving part; a 단순한 사람 is uncomplicated — compliment or verdict, tone decides). Band 6 words earn their rank by not being interchangeable.

強 strong — the hanja M56's 강조하다 note carried frozen finally lands its own word. 강한 팀 (M16's 팀), 강한 바람 (M11's 바람), 마음이 강해요 (M19's 마음). Radar, twice: M41's 세다 is the native muscle (힘이 세다 — arm-wrestling register); 강하다 is the Sino suit — teams, signals, wills. And M22's 강 is the river-江: the 한강 is long, not strong.

弱 weak — the third tenant on a busy syllable: NOT the medicine-藥 of M10's 약, NOT the promise-約 inside M5's 약속. 몸이 약해요 (M14's 몸) = frail; 커피를 약하게 (M1's 커피, the -게 adverb M33) = make it weak. 강하다's mirror — together they grade Wi-Fi bars, coffee, teams, and character.

深刻 deep-carved: serious the way an engraving is — it won't rub off. 심각한 문제 (M7's 문제), 병이 심각해요 (M14's 병). Radar vs M39's 심하다 (甚, over-the-line): 심하다 is HARSH — the friendship foul-call its note filed; 심각하다 is GRAVE — the doctor's face as the chart comes up. 감기가 심해요; 병이 심각해요.

Excellent, admirable — native through and through, no hanja to split, which suits a word this warm. 훌륭한 사람 (M1's 사람), 훌륭해요! = the teacher's highest praise, a full shelf above 좋아요. It praises character and work alike: essays, buildings, and grandchildren can all be 훌륭하다.

優秀: the excel-優 that fronts M51's 우승 (and M48's 배우) + a stand-out-秀 (frozen). Report-card register: 성적이 우수해요 (M35's 성적) = outstanding grades; 우수한 학생 (M4's 학생). The pair rule: 훌륭하다 admires, 우수하다 RANKS — one belongs in a speech, the other in a spreadsheet.

The word this course kept meeting frozen: M57's gap proverb 가는 말이 고와야 오는 말이 곱다 carried it 'untaught, riding frozen,' and M42's 미운 정 고운 정 rode it too. Thawed today: lovely, fine — 고운 목소리 (M19's 목소리), 마음이 곱다 (M19's 마음). ㅂ-irregular like M11's 덥다 family: 고와요, 고운. The grandmother's adjective — old-fashioned, fine-grained, warm.

The number-數 of M15's 수학 + 많다 (M7): countless. In practice badge-only: 수많은 사람들 (M1's 사람 wearing the plural -들, M27), 수많은 문제. Written register — headlines, history books, album liner notes; speech just reaches for M11's 정말 instead.

Off-the-wall, out of left field: 엉뚱한 질문 (M10's 질문), 엉뚱한 답 (M15's 답), 엉뚱한 곳에서 (M12's 곳) = in a completely unexpected place. Crucially FOND, not harsh — the class clown's adjective: wrong in an interesting direction. Half of Korean variety-show comedy is people being 엉뚱하다 on purpose.

en: to be any way whatever (in fixed frames)
notes: M29's 아무 — the indefinite system's front door — grown into an adjective that only lives in frames. 아무렇지 않아요 (the long negation -지 않다, M28) = I'm fine, unbothered: the brave face. 아무렇게나 (the -게 adverb M33, plus the opening -나 from 아무 때나) = any old way: 아무렇게나 하지 마세요 = don't just wing it. You will never meet it bare.

en: to be about that much; (verb) to stop doing
notes: Two readings, one spelling. The verb you can already assemble: M33's 그만 + 하다 = stop it — 그만하세요! (M33's note was already shouting it). The NIKL headword is the adjective: about-that-much — 그만한 사람이 없어요 = you won't find another like them; no one measures up. The gap deck banks the adjective's most famous frame.

en: to be on good terms, close
notes: M6's 사이 — whose note already taught 친구 사이 = '(we're) friends' — plus 좋다 (M1): the space between two people, in good repair. Mostly adverbial: 사이좋게 지내세요 (the -게 adverb M33, M23's 지내다) — the teacher's benediction over siblings and seatmates.

en: to be useless, of no use
notes: 所用 what-it's-for — the use-用 inside M10's 사용하다 — plus 없다 (M1): no use. 소용없어요 = there's no point; 울어도 소용없어요 = crying won't change it (the -아/어도 concession, M39, granting the tears and closing the door in one breath). Blunter than M7's 괜찮아요: not 'it's okay' but 'it won't matter.'

問題點: M7's 문제 + M32's 점 — the problem-POINT. A 문제 is the situation; a 문제점 is the specific thing wrong with it, which is what meetings exist to hunt: 문제점을 찾았어요 (M6's 찾다). 회의 (M10) after 회의, the list grows.

The native reason — M24's 이유 in hanbok. 까닭 없이 (M32's 없이) = for no reason at all; 무슨 까닭인지 (M10's 무슨, the indirect -는지 M33) = for some reason or other. Poetry, folktales, and grandmothers say 까닭; forms and small talk say 이유. Same question, two registers deep.

M29's 그 + the among-중 from S2, whose note already offered 이 중에서 = among these. 그중 runs the superlative frame M22 built: 그중에서 제일 좋아요 = of all of them, this one's best. Interviews, menus, and playlists all narrow down through 그중에서.

The 한 that 하나 (M5) wears before counters + M23's 쪽: one side. 한쪽 다리 (M14's 다리) = one leg; 한쪽 말만 듣지 마세요 (M30's 만, the -지 마세요 M14) = don't listen to only one side — fairness as geometry. The other side, when you need it, is 다른 쪽 — M29's 다른 doing the pointing.

量 amount — the ruler shelf M57 built (크기, 길이, 무게…) gains volume: 양이 많아요 = generous portions, the food-review verdict; 정확한 양 = the exact amount. Radar, a small government on one syllable: the 양 fronting M21's 양말 and M40's 양파 is Western-洋; the NIKL C-list adds sheep-羊 and both-兩; today's measure-量 is the one you'll say daily.

以外: the from-以 that fronts 이상 (M32) and 이하 (M39) + M55's 외 — other-than. 그 이외에 = besides that, everything else. Sign-and-form register like its parts: where speech says 그 외에 (M55's 외), documents stamp 이외. The 以-family now files up, down, and out.

最大 most-big: the most-最 ladder — 최고 (M19), 최근 (M32), 최선 (M39) — plus the big-大 of 대학교 (M15). 최대 세 명 (M5's counters) = three people at most; 최대한 = to the fullest possible (a limit-限 rides frozen): 최대한 빨리 (M12's 빨리) = as fast as humanly possible — the deadline's national adverb.

en: at the very least; the bare minimum
notes: 最小限 most-small-limit: the small-小 that 소설 (M48) and 소포 (M52) decoded, closing the 限 that 최대한 left frozen one line ago. The negotiation floor: 최소한 세 번 (M12's 번) = at least three times; 최소한의 예의 (M26's 예의) = the bare minimum of courtesy — the phrase dramas throw across dinner tables.

各種: M55's 각 — the written-notice each — + the seed-種 inside M57's 종류. 각종 서류 (M16's 서류) = every sort of paperwork; 각종 문제 = problems of every stripe. Notice-board register like both its parents; speech says 여러 종류 — M29's 여러 stacked on M57's 종류.
資 (funds) + 格 (rank): the paper that says you ARE allowed in — 자격이 없어요 (no clearance) is how a Korean office turns you away. A clean two-hanja split, no borrowed parts: both syllables stand new here.
制 (control) + 限 (limit). Radar: this 제 is 制 'control', a different hanja from M17's 제 'my' — same sound, different owner. The word a rule shrunk down to its ceiling.
違 (go against) + 反 (turn back). Radar: the 반 here is turn-back-反, NOT M15's 반 (the class) nor M24's 반대 (against) — same syllable, three jobs. The crossing of the line the rule-book exists to forbid.

命 (life) + 令 (deed): the thing handed down that is not a suggestion. The rung at the top of the rule ladder — an order you obey, a permission granted below it, a violation the moment you step past it.
申 (state) + 請 (ask to do): the paper you file when you want a thing done. First link in the office chain — 신청 (file), then 등록 (register), then 제출 (submit).
選 (pick) + 擇 (discern, then pick): both halves mean 'choose', which is why the word carries the whole act of deciding. The noun the decision verbs of this module swing around.

en: the credit; the standing to be trusted
notes: 信 (word-kept) + 用 (use). The 信 here is the 'letter/word' sense — not a feeling. Credit is exactly that: your reputation put to use when a bank lets you borrow.
强 (force) + 制 (control). Radar: the 강 here is force-强, a different hanja from M22's river-江 강 — the river is the river, the force is the fist. Coercion is control applied by strength, not consent.
交 (cross over) + 換 (swap). The 交 (crossing) is shared with 교류, but the second half decides it: 換 is a swap hand-for-hand, where 교류's 流 is a flow. Exchange vs. flow, same first syllable.

en: the registration; putting it on the books
notes: 登 (climb up) + 錄 (record): climbing your detail up onto the official record. The second link in the office chain, right after 신청 and before 제출.
確 (certain) + 認 (recognize). IOU: M20 taught 확인하다 as a verb; drop the -하다 and the bare noun finally stands — the check that a thing is real and in order.
要 (essential) + 請 (ask). The ask itself, as a thing you can pass around — 요청이 접수됐어요 (the request was logged).
報 (report) + 告 (tell). IOU: M43's 보고서 (the report-document) is this same 報告 with 서 'document' bolted on — the bare report, minus the paper, stands today.
IOU: M24 taught 반대 as a noun (against); attach the -하다 work and it becomes the act of opposing. One syllable, two parts of a sentence.
權 (authority) turned into 권 'suggest'. Radar: this 권 is 權 (power), NOT M5's 권 (the book-counter) — the authority here is the soft one: your right to nudge, never force, versus 강제's hard one.

en: to permit; to let it happen
notes: 許 (allow) + 容 (contain). The middle rung of the rule ladder: the order commands, the permission lets it through, the violation fires when you cross it.

en: to discuss; to weigh it out
notes: 論 (reason) + 議 (counsel): two minds reasoning a thing through, together. The verb you reach for when a choice is still a choice, not yet a rule.

en: to attempt; to try a plan
notes: 試 (test) + 圖 (plan): testing a plan that may not hold. 시도하다 is trying a course of action, not the M17 skill-row 잘하다/못하다 'good at / bad at'.

en: to apply a rule; to make it fit
notes: 適 (fit) + 用 (use): making a rule fit the case and putting it to work. The verb the rule-book runs on — 적용하다 is the act of a rule taking effect.

en: to relay; to hand it on
notes: 傳 (carry) + 達 (reach): carrying a thing from one desk to the next until it reaches. The office verb for passing a matter down the line.

en: to be in charge of; to own a duty
notes: 擔 (carry on the shoulder) + 當 (face): carrying a duty out in front. To 담당하다 a thing is to own it — the antonym of the thing being 무인 (nobody's).
進 (move forward) + 行 (do): moving a thing forward by doing. The verb for a meeting, a project, or a process running along.

en: to submit; to hand it up and out
notes: 提 (raise) + 出 (out): raising the paper and putting it out. The third link in the office chain — 신청, 등록, then 제출.

en: to attend; to take your seat
notes: 參 (mix in) + 席 (seat): mixing yourself in at the seat. 참석하다 is the formal 'to be present', not just 'to be there'.

en: to work the shift; to do duty
notes: IOU: M43 taught 근무 as a noun (duty, on the job); attach -하다 and it's the act of working the shift. The formal verb for on-duty work at a post.
IOU: M57 taught 활동 (activity) as a noun; -하다 makes it the act of being active, moving, running. 활동하다 is a person or a group in operation.
IOU: M33 taught 경험 (experience) as a noun; -하다 turns it into the act of going through it. 경험하다 is living the thing out to the other side.
勤 (diligent) + 勞 (labor) + 者 (one-who): the one who does diligent labor. Contrast M58's 노동자 (노동 'labor') — same person, 勤-勞 vs 動-勞; 근로자 is the formal register.
靑 (green) + 年 (year): the person in the green years. A clean split, both halves new — youth as an age, not a place.
人 (person) + 口 (mouth): people counted by their mouths. The word a census turns into a number.

en: the big firm; the major company
notes: 大 (big) + 企 (stand up to) + 業 (business). Radar: the 대 here is big-大, a different hanja from M55's 대 (the machine-/vehicle-counter, or 對 'versus'). The big firm is the big one, not the counted one.
外 (outside) + 交 (meeting): the meeting of outsiders, nations with nations. The 交 (crossing) is the same one as in 교환 and 교류 — crossing, but across borders.

en: the exchange; the running back and forth
notes: 交 (cross) + 流 (flow). Sibling of 교환: same 交 first syllable, but 流 is a flow and 換 a swap. 교류 lets two sides run into each other; 교환 hands one thing over.
집 (house) + 안 (M6's 안-inside): the inside of the house as an affair you run. 집안일이 많아요 — a lot of housekeeping on the plate. The 안 factory is already in your kit (M6), 집 the whole home (M1).

en: the household; the family (counted by mouths)
notes: 食 (eat) + 口 (mouth): the people who share the table. 식구가 많아요 — a big household. Radar: this 식 from 食 'eat' is not taught as a unit; M55's 식 (式, style) is a same-sound different-hanja owner.

en: the inner room; the master's room (traditionally the eldest's)
notes: 안 (M6's 안-inside) + 방 (M8's 방-room): the room kept inside the house — the head of the household's. In the old hanok layout this is where the eldest woman sits. 안방 is the room with the most weight, never the spare.

複 (two, doubled) + 道 (way): the passage that runs between the rooms. 복도를 걷다 — walk the hall (M6's 걷다). In an apartment, 복도 is the strip every room opens onto; in an office, the long strip with doors on both sides.

en: the window-outside; what you see through the glass
notes: 窓 (window) + 밖 (M6's 밖-outside): the outside, as measured from inside through the window. 창밖이 흐려요 — the window-outside is dim. The 창 syllable here is 窓 the window, not 倉 the warehouse of 창고 — same sound, different hanja.

室 (room) + 內 (inside): the inside of a building as one volume — 실내 vs. 실외 (inside / outside). 실내 온도 21도 — indoor temperature 21°. Radar: this 실 from 室 is frozen-and-glossed here; it is not a taught syllable yet.

en: the light-glow; the glow of a flame or lamp
notes: 불 (M13's 불-light) + 빛 (M49's 빛-light): the light itself, as a glow you can see. 불빛이 복도를 밝혀요 — a lamp-glow lighting the hall. Two light-words with different jobs: 불 is the flame, 빛 is the radiance.

en: the outside; outdoors (as opposed to indoors)
notes: A native Korean word, no hanja: the outside as a place, 바깥에 있어요 — be outdoors. Pairs with M6's 밖 (outside as a marker) — 밖 is the direction, 바깥 is the place. 바깥이 추워요 — it's cold out there.

en: in the water; what is under the surface
notes: 물 (M1's 물-water) + 속 (M28's 속-insides): the inside of the water. 물속이 차가워요 — the water's insides are cold. The X-속 factory: noun + 속 = inside the [noun], the deep-inside M28 owns. Not to be confused with 안 (M6's 안-inside) which is the boundary-enclosed side.

en: right in front of the eyes; at point-blank range
notes: 눈 (M14's 눈-eye) + 앞 (M6's 앞-front): the front of the eyes, i.e. right here. 눈앞에서 — at point-blank range. Radar: this 눈 from 目 eye is not M11's 눈-snow — same syllable, different hanja, two owners.

en: both sides; each side (of a pair)
notes: 兩 (both) + 쪽 (M23's 쪽-side): the two sides taken together. 양쪽 문이 열려요 — both doors open. Radar: this 양 from 兩 'both' is not M63's 양 (量, quantity) — a same-sound different-hanja pair.

en: the inner side; the inside (of a pair)
notes: 안 (M6's 안-inside) + 쪽 (M23's 쪽-side): the inside member of an outside-inside pair. 안쪽 창문 — the inside window. Opposite of 바깥쪽 (the outer side). The -쪽 direction factory reshells 안 into side-frame.

en: the back side; the rear (of a pair)
notes: 뒤 (M6's 뒤-back) + 쪽 (M23's 쪽-side): the back member of a front-back pair. 뒤쪽으로 — toward the rear. The -쪽 factory on top of the orientation noun: five directions in one stroke (위, 아래, 앞, 뒤, 안).

en: the above side; the upper part
notes: 위 (M6's 위-above) + 쪽 (M23's 쪽-side): the upper member of a below-above pair. 위쪽 벽 — the upper wall. Opposite of 아래쪽 (the lower side). 위 here is direction-above, not the M6 'on top of' marker that takes a noun (책상 위).

en: the below side; the lower part
notes: 아래 (M6's 아래-below) + 쪽 (M23's 쪽-side): the lower member of a below-above pair. 아래쪽 소파 — the lower sofa. Opposite of 위쪽. The -쪽 factory on M6's 아래.

en: the neighboring house; the house next door
notes: 옆 (M6's 옆-next-to) + 집 (M1's 집-house): the house on the next side. 옆집에서 소리가 나요 — sound from the next door. Not a compound in the dictionary sense; just a house measured by M6's 옆.

en: the next room; the adjoining room
notes: 옆 (M6's 옆-next-to) + 방 (M8's 방-room): the room on the next side, sharing a wall. 옆방에서 소리가 나와요 — a sound from the adjoining room. M6's 옆 + M8's 방, both already in your kit.

en: front-and-back; the two directions at once
notes: 앞 (M6's 앞-front) + 뒤 (M6's 뒤-back): the two cardinal directions held together. 앞뒤로 — in front and behind; 앞뒤가 바뀌어요 — the order flips. One word, a small axis.

앞 (M6's 앞-front) + 길 (M12's 길-road): the road as it runs in front of you. 앞길이 멀어요 — the road ahead is long. Opposite of 뒷길 (the road behind). M6's 앞 applied to M12's 길 — a road with a direction on it.

en: the front side; the forward direction (of a pair)
notes: 앞 (M6's 앞-front) + 쪽 (M23's 쪽-side): the front member of a front-back pair. 앞쪽 문 — the front door. Opposite of 뒤쪽. The -쪽 factory re-shells M6's 앞 into the side-frame.

en: in the chest; the insides of the heart-seat
notes: 가슴 (M30's 가슴-chest) + 속 (M28's 속-insides): the insides of the chest where feelings land. 가슴속이 아파요 — the chest's insides ache. The X-속 factory on a feeling-organ: noun + 속 = where it is felt.

en: in the head; what is running on in your mind
notes: 머리 (M8's 머리-head) + 속 (M28's 속-insides): the insides of the head. 머릿속이 어지러워요 — the head's insides are spinning. The X-속 factory on an organ: where thinking happens, made into a place.

en: in the dream; the inside of the dream-state
notes: 꿈 (M8's 꿈-dream) + 속 (M28's 속-insides): the inside of the dream. 꿈속에 나타나요 — appears in the dream. The X-속 factory on a state: a dream has an interior even if the body didn't.

倉 (granary, warehouse) + 庫 (store): a building for keeping things. 창고가 차요 — the warehouse is full. Radar: this 창 from 倉 'warehouse' is a different hanja from the 창 'window' in 창밖 — same syllable, two owners.

en: the branch (of an organization); the location (point on a map)
notes: 支 (support, branch-off) + 店 (shop): the branch — the 支 branch-off of a main 店 shop. This is the only (C) grade on the slice: NIKL's 지점01 支店 'branch' is rank 5557 grade-C, while 지점03 地點 'location' is rank 3298 grade-B. 두 가지 뜻 — two senses: the 支 branch (C, the shop you walk into) and the 地 location (B, a point on the map: 지도의 지점). Radar: don't confuse 지점 'branch' with 지점 'point' — same spelling, two hanja stacks.

en: the corner; the bent part of a room
notes: Loaned from English 'corner'. 코너에 있어요 — at the corner. In the room, the bent spot where two walls meet; in the street, the bent spot where two roads do. The corner of a room, a street, or a store aisle — and, pushed hard enough, the figurative one too (코너에 몰리다).
Loaned from English 'center'. 센터가 어디예요? — where is the hub? A service center is a 센터, a cultural center is a 센터, a call center is a 센터. Native Korean 중심 (center) still carries the formal weight.

en: the hall (of a school); the auditorium
notes: 講 (lecture) + 堂 (hall): the big room at a school for lectures and assemblies. 강당 문이 열려요 — the hall door is open. A 講- compound: the room that exists for the lecture to happen in.
Loaned from English 'campus'. 캠퍼스가 넓어요 — the campus is wide. Korean universities use the loan for the whole ground: buildings, roads, the 강당, the 교문, the 센터 — all of it is one 캠퍼스.

en: the school-gate; the main entrance of a school
notes: 校 (school) + 門 (gate): the gate that marks the school. 교문에서 만나요 — meet at the school gate. 校 'school' here is frozen-and-glossed (not yet taught as a root); 門 'gate' is a cognate of M6's 문 'door' — both are 門-stack.

en: the main gate; the front entrance
notes: 正 (main, correct) + 門 (gate): the main gate as opposed to a side gate. 정문으로 들어가세요 — enter through the main gate. Radar: this 정 from 正 'main' is a different hanja from M26's 정 (jeong, the feeling) — same sound, different owner. The 正 here means "correct / main / frontmost".

en: the entrance/exit door; the front door you go in and out of
notes: 出 (out) + 入 (in) + 門 (door): the door for going out and in. 출입문이 열려요 — the front door is open. Radar: this 入 'in' is frozen-and-glossed (not taught); do not confuse with M14's 입 'mouth' — same syllable, two different roots.

The view-blocker — a hand or a leaf set in front of the line of sight. NIKL lists two B-senses and both are yours: 시야를 가리다 (block the view) and 시비를 가리다 (settle right from wrong — M63's whole courtroom in one verb). 가리다 (block/settle) ≠ 가리키다 (point at) — same look, different hand jobs.
The pointing-finger verb — 손가락 (M28's 손가락) out, tip leading, the target named by direction. 가리키다 (point at) vs. 가리다 (block) is the module's cleanest look-alike split — one blocks, one names.
The fingers-in pick verb — M8's 손 closes in, thumb and two fingers, the thing leaving the surface. Same 집 as 뒤집다 (flip) — the fingers-act verbs.

The ground-pick verb — a walk, a stoop, a handful of leaves or crumbs coming up off the floor. 줍다 gathers up off the ground on the way; 집다 (M66) closes the fingers on the thing right in front of you — one pickup each, different roots.
The lift-from-the-container verb — a hand in, a ring on the hook, a fish out of M1's 물. 건지다 (lift out) reaches in and brings something up; 집다 (M66) just closes the fingers.

The drive-and-herd verb — 차를 몰다 drives the car (that 차 is M50's 자동차 clipped, not M2's 차 the tea), and the herd sense moves the whole flock at once. You met its passive in M65's 코너 note: 코너에 몰리다, driven into a corner.

en: to step aside; to make way
notes: The step-aside verb — 비켜! is what you hear when someone needs through: the body moves itself out of the path. 비키다 moves you, not the furniture — its object is your own position, cleared.
The shoulder-carry verb — the bag on M14's 어깨 (shoulder), the pail on the back. 메다 (shoulder-carry, M66) is a different root from M60's 매다 (tie) — same sound, different root, different hand.

The liquid-pour verb — M1's 물 over the lip of M18's 컵. ㅅ-irregular: 부어요 — the family's third member after 낫다 (M14) and 젓다 (M40). Radar twice: 얼굴이 붓다 (the face swells) is a second verb wearing this exact spelling, and M32's 따르다 also pours — 따르다 fills a glass for someone; 붓다 just moves the liquid.
The run-out spill verb — M1's 물 leaving its cup by accident, a streak down M6's 책상 (desk). 흘리다 is M35's 흐르다 (flow) with a hand on it: the flow, caused — and 쏟다 (M66) is the whole cup going over.
The overflow verb — a whole cup dumped on the floor, a sky opening and raining. 쏟다 (empty out, M66) is the heavy cousin of 흘리다 (spill, M66) — same root, different weight.

The laser-gun verb — an arrow, a beam, a look, all of them leaving the hand and aimed. 쏘다 (fire, M66) is also the treat-at-a-restaurant sense — the host sending the bill out at himself. Two aims, one verb.
The needle-in verb — a point against skin, a pin, the tip leading. 찌르다 (poke) is the sharp-tip version of a push; 집다 is the closed-fingers version — same hand, different tip. 르-family (M7): 찔러요.

The foot-swing kick verb — M14's 발 leading, the heel on M17's 공 (ball). Radar: four verbs wear this spelling — kick (공을 차다, today's), cold (바람이 차다 — also on your B-list, riding along here), full (가득 차다), and wear (시계를 차다). Different words, one face; the foot one is the headword.
The ground-tread verb — the sole of the shoe coming down on the leaf or the ball. 밟다 (step on) is the heavy cousin of 차다 (kick) — a foot either going through the ground or going at a thing.
The knock-on verb — the fist flat against M6's 문 (door), three taps, the sound inside answering. 두드리다 (knock, M66) is the deliberate version of a single pat — M8's 손, three strikes.
The burst-open verb — M36's 터지다 (burst) with the -뜨리다 make-it tail it shares with 떨어뜨리다: the pop, caused. Koreans 터뜨리다 balloons and feelings alike — a laugh, a cry, big news all burst open.
The make-it-drop verb — M36's 떨어지다 (fall) with the same -뜨리다 tail: fingers opening, M18's 컵 leaving the hand, the floor arriving first. The two M36 burst/fall verbs, each given a hand.

en: to run to (the 달려 + go compound)
notes: The run-to compound — M17's 달리다 (run) in its -어 coat, welded to M1's 가다 (go): running, going, one word.

en: to run here (the 달려 + come compound)
notes: The run-here compound — M17's 달리다 in its -어 coat + M1's 오다 (come). The opposite of 달려가다 (M66): same run, opposite direction.
The follow compound — M32's 따르다 (follow) in its -어 coat + M1's 가다 (go): the one behind, keeping pace.

en: to come after (the 따라 + come compound)
notes: The come-after compound — M32's 따르다 in its -어 coat + M1's 오다 (come). The opposite of 따라가다 (M66): you lead, they follow.
The flee verb — 달아 (the old run-stem) + M28's 나다 (emerge): running out and away. 달아나다 is the bolt; 도망가다 (M66) is the planned escape.
The escape verb — 도망 is 逃 (flee) + 亡 (vanish): run until you've vanished — plus M1's 가다. 도망가다 escapes from something; 달아나다 (M66) just bolts.

en: to give back (the 돌려 + give compound)
notes: The give-back compound — M37's 돌리다 (turn) in its -어 coat + M9's 주다 (give): turn it around and hand it back. The round trip in one verb.
The over-turn verb — the front face going over to the back. 뒤집다 (flip) is M6's 뒤 (back) + 집다 (pick up) — a back-facing pick-up.
The shake-off verb — the wrist loose, 먼지를 털다, the dust off the coat. Radar: M41's 털 (fur) shares the syllable — you 털다 the 털 off a jacket, which is all the mnemonic you need.

en: to put on top (the layer verb)
notes: The layer verb — 손을 얹다, a hand coming to rest on a shoulder; a plate set on the shelf's edge. Radar: 얹다 [언따] is one vowel from M9's 앉다 [안따] — setting a thing down on top vs. setting yourself down.

기쁘다 (M34) through the factory M42's 미워하다 filed: the adjective is your inside; the -아/어하다 verb is someone ELSE's outside, watchable. 합격 소식에 가족이 다 기뻐했어요 — you can't feel their 기쁘다, only watch their 기뻐하다. The ㅡ-drop comes pre-baked (기뻐-), so it runs like any 하다 verb: 기뻐해요, 기뻐했어요.

슬프다 (M7), acted out. Korean won't let you narrate a stranger's insides: 슬퍼요 is your own report; watching someone else, you say 슬퍼해요. 너무 슬퍼하지 마세요 — don't grieve too hard: -지 마세요 (M14) at its gentlest, aimed at sorrow you can see.

부럽다 (M24 — its note filed Korean envy as a warm compliment), performed: ㅂ softens to 워, then 하다 welds on. 부러워요 is what you say; 부러워하다 is what others can be seen doing — 친구들이 다 부러워해요 = the friends are all watchably jealous. Envy so public it conjugates.

즐겁다 (M29, ㅂ→워) from the outside: 아이들이 정말 즐거워해요 — you're reading the delight off their faces. The factory's four-pack is complete: 기뻐하다, 슬퍼하다, 부러워하다, 즐거워하다, one rule between them — adjective = felt, -아/어하다 = shown.

싸우다 (M19) + -(으)ㅁ: the fight, frozen solid enough to count. 부부 싸움 — M25's 부부 at war — is the proverbial one (a knife cutting water, says the proverb: it leaves no mark). And 눈싸움 splits on which 눈 you mean: M11's 눈 (snow) makes it a snowball fight; M14's 눈 (the eye), a staring contest.

만나다 (M2) + -ㅁ: vowel stems take the bare ㅁ, and the meeting becomes a thing that happens TO you: 만남이 있었어요. M46's 첫 makes it a drama premise — 첫 만남, the first meeting — and its bookend freezes M19's 헤어지다 the same way: 만남과 헤어짐, the pair every ballad is built on.

묻다 (M28) + -음 — and the ㄷ-irregular's ㄹ survives in the noun, exactly 걸음's rule (M38: 'the factory keeps fingerprints'). Register radar: mouths ask 질문 (M10); 물음 lives on the page — textbook headings, philosophy titles, and 물음표, the question mark itself.

어렵다 (M7) frozen: the ㅂ softens to 우 first, then the ㅁ lands — 어려움. The noun for hardship you can report having met: 어려움이 많았어요 = there were many difficulties — interview-Korean for a hard stretch, dignified where 고생 (M39) is raw.

어둡다 (M13), frozen and SHRUNK: 어둠, never 어두움 — the freezer occasionally seals a word at its shortest and the dictionary keeps it that way. 어둠 속에서 — the darkness housed in M28's 속 — = in the dark, where blackouts, horror films, and every metaphor for a bad year all live.

부끄럽다 (M34 — the blush that covers both shy and ashamed) at full length: ㅂ→우, no shrinking this time — compare 어둠, one entry up. 부끄러움이 많아요 = easily embarrassed, measured on the 많다-scale like everything Korean quantifies. The gap deck files its internet-era job.

en: to come to mind (a memory surfaces)
notes: 기억 (M34) + 나다 (M28): the memory erupts on its own — M34's 기억 note already ran the frame (기억이 나요), and M28's 나다 note listed this word the day the door was hung. Against M19's 기억하다: 기억하다 is you reaching; 기억나다 is it arriving. 이름이 기억 안 나요 — the name won't come, and no effort makes 나다 try harder.

en: to occur to one, pop into one's head
notes: 생각하다 (M10) minus its 하다, plus M28's 나다: a thought using the eruption door, no invitation needed. Broader than 기억나다, which surfaces your own past — 생각나다 also does cravings and missing people: 떡볶이가 생각나요 — M18's 떡볶이, suddenly urgent. Triggers, not effort.

en: to call to mind, summon (a thought)
notes: 떠오르다 (M49) through the causative party (M37): the thought that floats up on its own, now MADE to float — you summon it into 머릿속 (M65). The recall triangle closes: 기억하다 (M19) is effort, 기억나다/생각나다 are arrival, 떠올리다 is invocation. 르-family: 떠올려요.

The verb that exists to take 꿈 (M8) as its object: 꿈을 꾸다 — dream a dream, doubled exactly like 잠을 자다, per M28's 잠 note: 'Korean doubles up happily.' M32's 느끼다 note claimed -ㅁ built 꿈 from 꾸다; thirty-five modules later, here is the verb it was built from. Radar: a homograph 꾸다 borrows money (돈을 꾸다) — one dreams, the other owes.

꿈 (M8) + 꾸다, fused — and mostly promoted to daylight: 가수를 꿈꾸다 — M4's 가수, aspired to — = to dream of being a singer, the life-goal sense M8's 꿈 note filed. The night kind usually stays doubled (꿈을 꾸다); the fused verb aspires. 꿈꾸는 사람, wearing the badge (M24), is a dreamer.

想像: M34's 상상하다 promised 'the noun rides free' — collected. 상상이 안 돼요 = I can't picture it; 상상력 straps on the 력 M44's 능력 filed (M14's 힘 in a suit) and becomes imagination-as-capacity, the job-posting word. The hanja doubles the think-상 of 예상 (M34) — imagination is prediction unchained.

의심 (M34 — 疑心 doubt-heart) finally conjugates: that note pre-loaded 의심하지 마세요, and today the verb reports for duty, aimed at people and claims alike — the drama detective does little else all season. The heart-심 file (진심 M24, 관심 M24, 의심 M34) gains its biggest entry a few shelves down: 심리.

Strip the -스럽다 coat (the M45 factory) off 자랑스럽다 (M26) and the root stands bare, verbed: 자랑하다 = to show it off out loud. 아들 자랑 and 손자 자랑 — M4's 아들 and M47's 손자, bragged about — make it the national grandparent sport; 자랑스럽다 is the quiet glow, 자랑하다 the broadcast.

念慮 think-and-ponder: worry in its Sunday clothes. Radar vs 걱정하다 (M14), which frets in the kitchen — 염려하다 worries on letterhead: announcements, customer service, letters from institutions. 염려 마세요 is the polite deflection, softer and more formal than 걱정하지 마세요; the Sino noun 염려 rides along free beside 걱정 (M29).

en: to have a hard time, toil
notes: 고생 (M39 — 苦生 bitter-living) + 하다: to walk the hard road, not just name it. The gap deck (M26) already taught 고생했어요 — you've struggled well; stranger to English ears, 고생하세요 works as a goodbye to people still mid-shift. Korea honors effort by acknowledging its cost; this verb does the acknowledging.

Native, no hanja, no English equivalent: the felt worth of effort — what fills you when the hard thing turns out to have mattered. Measured on the 있다-chassis (보람이 있어요/없어요) and felt through M32's 느끼다: 보람을 느껴요. Jobs, parenting, and language apps are all audited in 보람; may yours run a surplus.

興味 rise-flavor: the 미 is the flavor-味 of 의미 (M32) — interest as a taste that rises in you. Radar vs M24's 관심: 관심 points at people and things (관심 있어요 starts relationships); 흥미 points at topics and fields — 역사에 흥미가 있어요, with M15's 역사 as the topic. Textbooks measure it on the same chassis: 흥미가 있다/없다.

The body's battery reading. Radar vs M14's 힘: 힘 is muscle you apply; 기운 is the charge you woke up with — 기운이 없어요 = drained, the whole-system cousin of the universal symptom M14's 힘 note filed. 감기 기운 — M14's 감기, at first hum — = a touch of a cold; 기운 내세요 = the gentler 힘내세요.

心理 heart-logic: the heart-심 file M34's 의심 note built (진심/관심 M24, 의심 M34) meets the ordering-理 of 정리 (M54) — the heart's filing system, studied as a field. 심리 테스트 is the personality quiz Korea loves; add the field-학 M44's 문학 collected and 심리학 is the university department. Says 심니 — the ㄹ assimilating, as 정리 already showed.

Konglish radar: a 콤플렉스 is an insecurity about one specific FEATURE — 키 콤플렉스, built on M27's 키 — not English 'complicated,' and only distantly Freud. 콤플렉스가 있어요 confesses the soft spot; naming someone else's is a line you don't cross. The loanword arrived clinical and went personal.

M53's 피로 (疲勞 worn-labor), conjugated. Radar vs 피곤하다 (M7): 피곤해요 is what your mouth says at day's end; 피로하다 is what the pharmacy poster and the health column write — 눈이 피로할 때 = for tired eyes, per every eye-drop box. Speech keeps 피곤하다; print prefers the lab coat.

不幸: the 불- ledger M42's 불만 note told you to keep (불가능, 불편, 불안, 불만) now stamps fortune itself — the 행 of 행복하다 (M7) and 다행 (M36). The gap deck (M36) already built it into 불행 중 다행; today the adjective stands alone. 불행하게도 — unfortunately — opens bad news the way 다행히 opens good.

크다 (M1) wearing the badge (M24) + the work-일 inside M2's 일하다: a big matter — and in speech, almost always a bad one. 큰일 났어요! = we're in trouble: the 났- is M28's 나다, a crisis erupting through the same door feelings use. Said 큰닐, with the wedged-in ㄴ that 나뭇잎 (M49) also wears. The sincere sense survives in 큰일을 하다 = to do great work.

Literally what-matter, actually a greeting: 웬일이에요? = what brings YOU here?! — said to the friend who never visits, the coworker holding coffee for once. It requests no information; it performs the delighted double-take. Radar: 무슨 일이에요? (M10's 무슨) genuinely asks what happened; 웬일이에요? celebrates that it did. Says 웬닐 — 큰일's rule again.

The IOU comes due: M41's 흔들다 note used it free — 고개를 흔들다 = shake the head no, with 고개, 'the head-as-it-turns,' riding along — and M41's 숙이다 runs on 고개를 숙이다. Now it's taught, with the full collocation row: 고개를 끄덕이다 (nod — next entry) / 흔들다 (M41) / 숙이다 (M41) / 돌리다 (M37 — look away). Radar vs M14's 목: 목 is the anatomical neck-and-throat that gets sore; 고개 is the head as it MOVES. Second sense on the ledger: a 고개 is also a mountain pass — the 아리랑 고개 of the song — which you cross with M36's 넘다.

고개를 끄덕이다 = nod yes — the agreement gesture, cousin of the mimetic 끄덕끄덕 (the head's bob-bob, riding free and glossed). The polite form contracts: 끄덕여요, 끄덕였어요. The no-side is already yours: M41's 흔들다 swings the head sideways, and M40's 젓다 filed 고개를 젓다 = shake your head no. Yes bobs; no swings.

en: to stare at, look up at
notes: The -보다 gaze fleet — M15's 물어보다, M49's 바라보다, M50's 둘러보다, M52's 돌아보다, M56's 살펴보다, M61's 찾아보다 — commissions its bluntest ship: fix your eyes on something and HOLD. 왜 쳐다봐요? = why are you staring? Held on a person it turns rude fast — Korean politeness points eyes down, not at — but aimed upward it's innocent: 하늘을 쳐다보다 (M11's 하늘).

M6's 내리다 (down) welded into the fleet: look DOWN at — 산 위에서 도시를 내려다보다, the observation-deck verb. Same social edge as English: 사람을 내려다보다 = look down ON someone, altitude as attitude. The gaze goes where the body sits: this verb requires you to be higher first.

en: to peer into, look closely at
notes: Peer INTO: M28's 들다 in its enter sense — its note said the 들 inside 들어가다 meant entering was its first job all along — aimed through 보다, so the eyes go inside. 거울을 들여다보다 (M13's mirror), 핸드폰만 들여다보다 (M6's phone — the era's default posture), and the desk job: examine closely — 문제를 들여다보다 (M7's 문제) is what a careful reader does to a contract.

The face-to-face adverb (shelved as a noun by house rule): set it before a verb and the action happens front-to-front — 마주 보다 (M1's 보다 — lock eyes), 마주 서다 (M14's 서다), 마주 앉다 (M9's 앉다 — across the table, where interviews and first dates live). No particle, no conjugation: 마주 just walks up to the verb and faces it.

M50's 다가오다 promised this mirror by name — 다가가다 'approaches AWAY from you' — and here it lands: close the distance, step by careful step, from you toward the target. 아기에게 천천히 다가가다 (M25's 아기); goals and people take the same slow approach. The compass holds: 오다-compounds come at me, 가다-compounds go from me.

en: to turn away, turn one's back
notes: M37's 돌다 (turn) + M14's 서다 (stand): pivot until your back is the conversation — the exit gesture. 그냥 돌아서서 갔어요 = just turned and walked away. Hearts run it too: 마음이 돌아서다 (M19's 마음) = affection turns for good, the breakup verb dramas dread. Radar vs M52's 돌아보다: 돌아보다 turns to LOOK back; 돌아서다 turns to LEAVE.

The confront-맞 of M15's 맞다 — the receiving end its note filed with 주사를 맞다 — + M14's 서다: stand to take it, feet planted AGAINST. 문제에 맞서다 (M7's 문제) = face the problem down; people, storms, and unfair rules all sit in the 에/에게 slot. One notch past 마주: 마주 서다 faces; 맞서다 opposes.

en: to be ahead, go in front
notes: M6's 앞 + M14's 서다: stand at the front = be ahead — 선수가 앞서다 (M17's 선수, leading the race), scores, technologies, worries that run ahead of the facts. Its fossil 앞서 (beforehand — riding free and glossed) opens formal sentences: 앞서 말한 것처럼 = as mentioned earlier, M4's 말하다 framed by M41's 처럼.

M36's 넘다 (cross over) + M14's 서다: cross AND stand on the far side. Literal on this module's own noun — 고개를 넘어서다, past the mountain pass — and figurative on M26's 목표: 목표를 넘어서다 = surpass the goal. 넘다 is mid-crossing; 넘어서다 has landed beyond and planted a flag.

The 뛰어- squadron opens on M66's chassis — the weld that built 달려가다 and 따라오다, now with M28's 뛰다 as the engine. Here it bolts to M28's 들다 (the enter-들 of 들어가다): leap INTO — 바다에 뛰어들다 (M11's 바다), and headfirst life choices: plunging into a new field is the same dive. ㄹ-stem in the polite forms: 뛰어들어요, and the ㄹ drops before ㅅ — 뛰어드세요.
뛰다 + M8's 나가다: burst OUT — the school-bell verb, what 아이들 do to a 교실 (M15) the second M8's 끝나다 fires. Same chassis, outbound: the door is a formality when the body is already running.

뛰다 + M1's 오다: arrive at a run — the friend who heard the news, the 강아지 (M22) who heard the food bowl. M66's 달려오다 sprints in on 달리다's track legs; 뛰어오다 hustles in on 뛰다's everyday ones — same doorway, different gait.

뛰다 + M16's 다니다, the routine-going verb: run AROUND — motion with mileage but no destination. 아이들이 집 안에서 뛰어다녀요 (M6's 안) is the downstairs neighbor's whole complaint; adults do it on errands, 뛰어다니면서 between offices all week. 다니다 supplies the rounds; 뛰다 sets the pace.

M28's 날다 + M1's 오다: come FLYING in — 공이 날아오다 (M17's 공: duck), 새가 날아오다 (M22's 새). Wingless things fly too: questions, 소문 (M24 — rumors travel airborne), and the occasional classroom chalk. If it arrives faster than it should, Korean gives it wings.

M12's 건너다 (cross the road) + M1's 오다: cross to THIS side — 길을 건너오다 (M12's 길), waved over from across the street. Scale it up and it carries history: 바다를 건너오다 (M11's 바다) is how loanwords, recipes, and grandparents arrived. The compound always ends where you stand.

The raise-verb 올리다 (M20 — 'literally to raise,' its note said, before the internet borrowed it; M22's 오르다 pushed through M37's causative party) + M28's 놓다: lift UP onto a surface and leave it there — 가방을 책상 위에 올려놓다 (M6's 위). File the split: M40's -아/어 놓다 is 놓다 doing GRAMMAR (do-and-leave-standing); 올려놓다 is 놓다 doing vocabulary — a physical weld, not an aspect.

M6's 내리다 + M28's 놓다: lower it and let it rest — 가방을 내려놓다, 컵을 내려놓다 (M18's 컵). The second job is monastic: 마음을 내려놓다 (M19's 마음) = set the heart down = let it go, Korea's favorite consolation verb. Same split as its twin above: the compound is vocabulary; M40's -아/어 놓다 is grammar.

M6's 오른쪽 + M8's 손, fused: the right hand — first cell of a four-cell grid built from zero new roots. It's the polite hand: things pass to elders in the 오른손 (or both hands), never the left alone, and 악수 below is strictly its job.

M6's 왼쪽 + M8's 손: the left hand — the support crew, tucked under the right forearm when you pour for or hand things to an elder. A left-hander is a 왼손잡이 (riding free and glossed) — the same thing-you-grab build as 손잡이 below, aimed at a person.

M6's 오른쪽 + M14's 발: the right foot — the grid's third cell, and most people's default: the first step onto the stairs, the plant foot, the pedal foot. 축구 (M17) files every player by this noun and the next one.

M6's 왼쪽 + M14's 발: the left foot — in 축구 the scarce resource: a 왼발을 잘 쓰는 선수 (M17's 선수) gets scouted on that phrase alone. Dance classes count 오른발, 왼발 out loud; the grid closes at four cells, zero new roots.

M8's 손 + M14's 발 run as one unit: the working extremities — and Korean's teamwork gauge. 손발이 맞다 (M15's 맞다) = our hands-and-feet fit = we click without talking; the gap deck files the full idiom. Winter's version is literal: 손발이 차가워요 (M18's 차갑다) — the extremities report the season first.

M8's 손 + M28's 잡다 + noun-making -이: the thing-you-grab = handle — 문 손잡이 (M6's 문), 지하철 손잡이 (M6's 지하철: the swaying loop commuters trust their mornings to). Radar on the suffix: M57's 높이 runs the measure--이 (high-ness = height); this -이 builds a THING. Same letter, different factory.

M8's 손 + M30's 수건: the HAND towel = handkerchief. Old-school kit: pinned to a kindergartener's chest, waved from train platforms (M41's 흔들다 has the wave), passed wordlessly in dramas whenever someone cries. A gift that says neat, tidy, slightly retro.

The native clap: 손뼉을 치다 (M17's 치다, the strike-play verb) = clap your hands — palms meeting, the sound itself. Radar vs M51's 박수: 박수 is the hanja clap and the applause EVENT (you send it, you receive it — 박수를 받다); 손뼉 is the PALMS. 손뼉을 치면서 웃다 (M7's 웃다) is the full-body Korean laugh.

握手 grab-hand: the 악 is grab — what M28's 잡다 does, written in hanja — and the 수 is the hand-手 that M37's 세수 filed and M51's 박수 confirmed. 악수하다 rides free: shake with the 오른손, always, 왼손 under the forearm when respect is due. Business Korea bows and shakes at the same time — do both, slightly, and you can't miss.

The act-noun with a curled lip: 그런 짓 하지 마세요 (M24's 그런; -지 마세요 from M14) = don't DO that kind of thing — a 짓 is almost always regrettable. Neutral cousins ride free and glossed: 손짓 (hand signal), 몸짓 (body gesture — M14's 몸). Radar: NO relation to M54's 짓다 the build-verb — 짓다 builds rice and houses; 짓 just misbehaves.

宗敎 lineage-teaching: religion itself — a new hanja 宗 (a root line, an ancestral house) plus the teach-敎 of 교회/교수 (M27) and 교육 (M32). Korea files its faiths as teachings, and the two entries below take the word literally. Radar: M32's 교육 note flagged it first — 학교's 교 is the school-building 校, not this one.

佛敎 Buddha-teaching: Korea's oldest organized 종교, fifteen centuries in — headquartered in the mountain 절 (M26), visible in every 탑. The 불 is Buddha-佛, your third 불: M13's fire, the not-不 of 불가능하다 (M39), and now the Buddha. About a fifth of the country practices; the vocabulary belongs to everyone.

儒敎 scholar-teaching: the system of 공자 (Confucius — riding frozen) that governed Joseon for five centuries. M44's 유학 note filed the homograph 유학 (儒學, Confucian studies) — same scholar-儒, now wearing 敎. Less a Sunday 종교 than an operating system: 웃어른 first, 조상 remembered, 존댓말 (M19) always — you've been practicing 유교 since M4's swap table.

The Buddha — nearly always 부처님 in speech, wearing the -님 of 선생님 (M4); M16's 님-ladder reaches all the way up. The hanja 佛 spells him in 불교. Radar from the news: a homograph 부처 (部處) means government ministries — 정부 (M32) 부처 — sharing nothing with the temple but sound.

The Buddhist monk — with the -님 built in at the factory: there is no plain form to subtract, the respect ships with the word. Address one directly as 스님, the way 선생님 (M4) works for teachers. Gray robes, a mountain 절 (M26), and a workday that starts in the 새벽 (M38) — the temple wakes before the buses do.

塔: the stone pagoda in the 절 마당 (M54's 마당, at its most solemn) — layered stories of 돌 (M22), often a millennium old and still standing where the courtyard paths cross. One of them rides in your pocket: 다보탑 (frozen — a National Treasure) is the design on the 10-won coin. Pilgrims still circle them slowly clockwise — 탑돌이, the pagoda-walk, M37's 돌다 on sacred duty.

牧師 shepherd-teacher: the Protestant pastor — the 牧 tends flocks, the 師 teaches them, and the job description writes itself. He works at the 교회 (M27), under one of the red crosses that note said light the skyline; address him as 목사님, because M16's 님-ladder covers clergy too. His Catholic colleague is a different word — M47's 신부 note already met the priest (神父).

神: a god — or God: 신을 믿다 (M19's 믿다) = to believe in one; 하느님/하나님, the Korean names for the capital-G version, ride frozen. You met the hanja in M47's 신부 note — the Catholic priest is 神父, a god-father. Radar, twice: 신다 (M21) and 신발 (M9) are unrelated shoes, and the everyday OTHER 신 is native excitement — 신이 나다 = to be having a blast (M28's 나다, erupting joy), 신나는 노래 = an upbeat song.

祈禱 entreat-entreat: both hanja mean pray — the word doubles down, and 기도하다 rides free. Every door on this shelf runs it: 손을 모으다 (M8's 손, M17's 모으다 — hands gathered) at the 절, heads bowed at the 교회, and 새벽 기도 — dawn prayer, M38's hour — filling pews before the commute. To ask BIG, Korean also switches verbs: that one is next.

en: to wish, pray for; to beg (forgiveness)
notes: To wish — and to beg: you 빌다 a 소원 (a wish — riding frozen) to the moon or the 조상, and you 빌다 forgiveness when the 잘못 (M63) was yours: 잘못을 빌다. ㄹ-stem manners: 빌어요, but the ㄹ bows out before ㅅ — 비세요. One syllable from its neighbor below; keep them apart and you'll never accidentally borrow a blessing.

To borrow: 돈을 빌리다 (M9's 돈), 책을 빌리다 — and with M9's 주다 welded on, 빌려주다 = to lend. The polite form contracts: 빌려요, never 빌리어요. The module's sharpest radar: 빌다 asks heaven, 빌리다 asks the bank — the extra 리 is the entire difference.

祖上 forebears-above: the ancestors — the people upstream of your family line, greeted at every 명절 (M25). M46's 차례 note already set their table (茶禮, the dawn rite); M63's gap deck already blamed them (못되면 조상 탓, with this word riding frozen) — today it lands for real. The evening version of the rite, 제사 (the memorial — riding frozen), keeps them fed year-round.

還甲 the-cycle-returns: the traditional calendar runs on a sixty-year cycle, and 환갑 is the birthday it comes full circle — your birth year RETURNS. M30's 예순 note promised this word ('the year before 환갑'); the feast is the 환갑 잔치, M25's 잔치 at its most filial. Once a survival milestone with a village-scale party — modern medicine demoted the miracle, but the family still gathers.

웃- (the old 'upper' combining form of 위, M6) + 어른 (M24): one's elders as a class — the people above you, whom you greet first, serve first, and 뵙다 (M47) rather than merely 보다. Said 우더른. The whole 존댓말 apparatus (M19) exists for them; so does half of this module's bowing.

모이다 (M25) through the -ㅁ factory (M33's 웃음 named the machine; M38's 걸음 joined it): the gathering, nouned — and M25's note promised this exact word: '모임 — a meetup — is this verb turned noun.' Paid in full. Book clubs, church small groups, alumni dinners — any recurring get-together; 오늘 모임이 있어요 is the standing Korean evening plan.

行事 go-affair: the organized event — 학교 행사, 회사 행사, banners and a schedule. Both halves are veterans: the go-行 of 행동 (M57), the affair-事 of 사건 (M36) and 사업 (M43). You 열다 (M13) a 행사 — open it like a door. Radar: a formal homograph 행사 (行使) is the exercising of a right — 권리를 행사하다 (권리 = a right, riding frozen) — election-news Korean, no banners involved.

The campus club — a rare native word on this hanja shelf. Sort the gathering radar: 단체 (M23) is the formal organization, 파티 (M19) is one night, a 모임 is any meetup — a 동아리 is BELONGING: weekly 동아리 활동 (M57's 활동), a shared clubroom, seniors who buy the dinner. Korean university life is sorted by which one you joined.

同窓 same-window: you sat by the same classroom 창문 (M6) — the window-窓 that M65's 창밖 filed — under the same-同 of 동시 (M38). A schoolmate from back then, forever. 동창회 — add the gathering-회 that M27's 교회 note decoded — is the reunion where everyone measures everyone; in Korea, 동창 networks find people jobs and spouses decades later.

Konglish radar, the classic: 미팅 is the GROUP BLIND DATE — N friends, N strangers, one long café table, arranged by a mutual friend; university folklore since your parents' generation. The business meeting is 회의 (M10 — 'the eternal office excuse'). Offices have lately borrowed 미팅 back for meetings, but the dictionary — and every campus drama — holds the line: it's a date.

祝賀 bless-celebrate: the congratulation itself — completing 축하하다 (M19), whose note taught you it's said 추카, the ㅎ-merge live. The bare noun stacks onto everything: 축하 파티, 축하 인사말, 축하를 받다 (M9's 받다, at its happiest). Korea does congratulation as an event — there is always cake.

歡迎 joy-greet: the welcome — 환영합니다! hangs over airport gates, store doors, and first days; 환영하다 rides free. Add the gathering-회 that M27's 교회 note filed and 환영회 is the welcome party every 신입생 (M58) gets. Radar, in-module: 환영's 환 is joy-歡, 환갑's 환 is return-還 — two 환s, one module, different hanja.

招請狀 invite-request-document: the formal invitation card. 초대하다 (M19) is how you invite friends; 초청 is the podium register — ceremonies, embassies, keynote speakers. The -장 is document-狀, NOT M30's flat-thing counter 장 — though the card it names is still, maddeningly, 한 장. The wedding one has its own word: 청첩장, riding frozen.

인사하다's 인사 (M19 — 'the greeting itself, bow included') + 말 (M4): greeting-words — the short prepared speech at a wedding, a first day of work, the opening of a 모임. 축하 인사말 is the toast; 새해 (M25) 인사말 is the New Year address. Korea scripts its warmth, and this is the word for the script.

어린이 (M35) + 날 (M11): Children's Day, May 5 — a national day off on which the kids outrank everyone. M35's note already told the story: 방정환 coined 어린이 to dignify children, then founded this holiday for them. It slots into the -날 shelf beside M25's 한글날 and 어버이날 — May in Korea is one long family gauntlet.

德分 virtue-portion: 덕수궁's virtue-德 (M31) + 부분's portion-分 (M32) — your share of someone else's goodness. [Person] 덕분에 = thanks to them, and it ONLY credits: M29's 때문 note said 'credit or blame; tone decides' — 덕분 pre-decided. 동창 덕분에 취직했어요 (M43's 취직); and when someone asks how you've been, the gap deck holds the politest answer in Korean.

M7's 높다 — 'Buildings and mountains, not people' — on the conveyor: 높아지다 = to get higher. The polite form is just the parent's 높아요 with 지다 welded on: 높아져요, 높아졌어요. Prices and temperatures ride it most — 가격이 높아졌어요 (M21's 가격), 기온이 높아지다 (M49's 기온) — and so does the bar: 목표가 높아졌어요 (M26's 목표).

M7's 많다 through the conveyor — and the M35 md already ran this exact word as its example (많아지고 있어요 — 'there's more and more'); today it takes a seat. The parent's silent ㅎ stays silent: 많아져요 says 마나져요. Count anything: 사람이 많아지다, 일이 많아지다 (M2's 일), 외국인이 많아지고 있어요 (M23's 외국인) — the -고 있다 progressive from M8 stacks on, exactly as M35 said it would.

M6's 멀다 (멀어요) plus 지다: distance increasing — 집에서 점점 멀어져요 as the bus pulls away (M1's 집, M35's 점점). But its real job is hearts: 마음이 멀어지다 (M19's 마음) = to drift apart, 친구하고 멀어졌어요 = we grew apart. The proverb that runs it twice — out of sight, out of mind — waits in the gap deck.

Receipt, paid: M42's 익숙하다 promised this word by name — 'The workhorse form is 익숙해지다 = to GET used to' — and the M42 sentence deck already conjugated it (지금은 익숙해졌어요). Hada-adjectives ride the conveyor through 해: 익숙해요 → 익숙해져요. Keep the 에 the parent note insisted on: 한국 생활에 익숙해졌어요 (M29's 생활) — you get used TO a thing.

M13's 넓다 taught the ㄼ dance — 널따 before a consonant, but 'both letters wake with a vowel: 넓어요 (neolbeoyo)' — so the conveyor form keeps both awake: 넓어져요. Roads widen (길이 넓어졌어요, M12's 길), and so do people: 시야가 넓어지다 (시야, field of view — riding frozen) is the compliment travel earns; 마음이 넓어지다 (M19's 마음) the one age does.

M6's 가깝다 conjugates ㅂ-irregular (가까워요) and the 워 survives inside the change-verb — 가까워지다 — the same 'two machines at once' M35's 달라지다 note filed for the 르-family. Time and people both: 시험 날짜가 가까워져요 (M10's 시험, M25's 날짜) = the exam is coming up; 친구하고 가까워졌어요 = we got close. 멀어지다's mirror, and Korea's word for a friendship deepening.

M7's 짧다 — 'the buried ㅂ surfaces' in 짧아요 — so it surfaces here too: 짧아지다, jjalbajida. Days do it every autumn (해가 짧아졌어요 — M11's 해, the sun's hours shrinking), and so does hair after 자르다 (M40): 머리가 짧아졌네요 (M8's 머리), noticed with the -네요 from M26. Radar: 짧다 is length; for amounts, see 적어지다 two shelves down.

M1's 작다 (작아요, jagayo) on the conveyor: SIZE shrinking — 옷이 작아졌어요 (M7's 옷: the clothes got small, which is how Korean says you didn't) — and 소리가 작아지다 (M19's 소리), the volume going down. Radar pair with the next entry: 작아지다 shrinks a size, 적어지다 shrinks an amount — M1 vs M7 is the whole difference.

M7's 적다 (적어요) plus 지다: the AMOUNT goes down — 손님이 적어졌어요 (M9's 손님: fewer customers), 돈이 적어지다 (M9's 돈). It is 많아지다's exact mirror, and the radar's twin of 작아지다: a room gets 작아지다, the people in it get 적어지다. Korean keeps count and size apart at the root; the conveyor doesn't merge them.

M13's 어둡다 — 'ㅂ-irregular: 어두워요. Joins the 덥다/춥다/맵다 family' — so the 워 rides inside: 어두워지다. The evening's verb: 날이 어두워지면 (M11's 날, with -(으)면 from M20) = when it gets dark. Faces too: 표정이 어두워졌어요 (M34's 표정) = their face fell. M67's 어둠 froze the darkness itself; this is the darkness arriving.

en: to come to dislike, go off
notes: M3's 싫다 (싫어요, sireoyo) on the conveyor: coming to hate — 그 노래가 싫어졌어요 (M7's 노래) = I've gone off that song. The mirror of M53's 좋아지다, whose note ran '그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I've come to like them': swap the adjective and 싫어졌어요 = I've come to hate it. Same subject marker, same machine, opposite verdict — and 다 싫어졌어요 (M9's 다) is the burnout confession.

M66's 쏟다 — 'the overflow verb' — through the -지다 wing of the party, the wing the M36 md named while seating 깨지다, 켜지다, 꺼지다, 사라지다. You 쏟다 the cup; the sky 쏟아지다-s: 비가 쏟아져요 = rain pours down (M11's 비). Also applause and tears — 박수가 쏟아졌어요 (M51's 박수) = the applause came pouring, 눈물이 쏟아지다 (M14's 눈물). The gap deck files what sleep does with it.

en: to come true, be achieved (contracted form)
notes: M35's 이루어지다 with one syllable squeezed out: 우 + 어 → 워, the squeeze M2's 배우다 note taught (배워요). Print prefers the short form; NIKL lists both, so the ledger seats both. Everything that note taught still holds — '꿈은 이루어진다 = dreams come true — the 2002 World Cup's national slogan' — and 꿈이 이뤄졌어요 (M8's 꿈) says it in five syllables. M35's 이루다 does; 이뤄지다 happens.

펼치다 (to spread out, unfold — riding frozen, untaught) through the -지다 wing: the thing unfolds ITSELF. The view opens: 경치가 펼쳐져요 (M22's 경치) = the scenery spreads out before you — the 등산 summit sentence (M17's 등산); and events unroll: 축제가 펼쳐지다 (M25's 축제). The 쳐 arrives pre-contracted (치 + 어), so the sound is pyeolchyeo.

en: to be passed along, be handed down
notes: M33's 전하다 (傳 transmit — '말을 전해요 (pass the word along)') flipped: the word travels on its own. 소식이 전해졌어요 (M20's 소식) = word got through; 옛날부터 전해지는 이야기 (M24's 옛날, M24's 이야기, wearing the badge from M24) = a story handed down. The hada-verb converts through 해, so the wing form is 전해지다 — the mirror of 익숙해지다 on the adjective side.

M12 taught 세우다 as the taxi's pull-over ('세워 주세요 — please pull over'); the M37 md then decoded it — '= 서다 + 이우 — parking is making the car stand.' Aim the same make-stand verb at a building (건물을 세우다, M22's 건물) or a plan (계획을 세우다, M8's 계획), and the wing form reports the result: 탑이 세워졌어요 (M69's 탑) = the pagoda was erected; 계획이 세워지다 = a plan gets drawn up.

en: to be drawn; to come to the mind's eye
notes: M15's 그리다 ('그림을 그려요 — draw a drawing') turned around: 그림이 그려지다 = the picture gets drawn. Second job, the mind's eye: 그 장면이 아직도 그려져요 (M48's 장면, M14's 아직) = I can still picture the scene — the image draws itself in you. The 려 is the parent's own -어 form (그려), with 지다 welded on.

M33's 정하다 — 'the smallest decision machine Korean sells' — in its happen-form: the date sets itself. 날짜가 정해졌어요 (M25's 날짜) = the date's been fixed; 정해진 시간 wears the badge from M24 = the appointed time; 아직 안 정해졌어요 = not decided yet (M14's 아직, M3's 안). Beside 결정되다 on the shelf below: 정해지다 for the small settings, 결정되다 for the heavy rulings — the same weight split the parents had.

en: to snap, break off (on its own)
notes: M20's 끊다 (전화를 끊다 — end the call) gets a SECOND passive — the party's twin-invitation case. M36's 끊기다 (the 기-row of the M36 table: 끊다 → 끊기다) is cut off BY something: '전화가 끊겼어요 = the call dropped', and M36's 전기 note ran 전기가 끊겼어요. 끊어지다 snaps on its own: 줄이 끊어졌어요 (M55's 줄, the rope) = the rope gave way; 연락이 끊어지다 (연락 — the noun inside M19's 연락하다) = to lose touch. Two passives, one parent: 기 blames a hand, 어지다 blames time.

M33's 결정하다 ('결정했어요! = I've decided') through the move M36 named — 'swap the 하다, get the happen-form' — with M57's 결정 as the noun in the middle. 결정됐어요 = it's been decided, no decider named: the committee's tense. 아직 결정 안 됐어요 splits the verb around M3's 안, exactly where M57's 결정 note left 아직 결정 못 했어요.

Receipt, paid: M56's 포함하다 note already ran the passive and named the machine — 'Usually met wrapped itself, in the 되다-machine (M36): 아침 식사가 가격에 포함되어 있어요'. Today the word gets its own seat: X이/가 Y에 포함되다 = X is included in Y, and the -어 있어요 tail keeps it in the included STATE — which is why hotels and price lists say 포함되어 있어요 far more than 포함돼요. 세금 포함 (M43's 세금) on a receipt is the bare noun doing the same job.

M56's 마련하다 (자리를 마련하다; the headline's 대책을 마련하다, with 대책 riding frozen there as here) flipped: the provision appears without a provider. 자리가 마련됐어요 (M12's 자리) = a spot has been set up — the host's sentence; 대책이 마련되다 = measures are put in place — the government's. Native root, Sino machine: 되다 doesn't check pedigree, only the 하다 it replaces.

M16's 소개하다 (소개해 주세요 — set me up) and M33's 소개 (紹介) in the happen-form: to get introduced — mostly by the media. 티비에 소개된 맛집 (M8's 티비, M18's 맛집, badge from M24) = the restaurant that got featured on TV, which in Korea means a line down the block by the weekend. 이 책은 한국에 처음 소개됐어요 (M15's 처음) = was first introduced to Korea.

M36 named it among the 되다-verbs (시작되다, 준비되다, 걱정되다); M53's 걱정되다 cleared its IOU from that same list, and today 준비되다 clears its own. M8's 준비하다 gets you ready FOR something; 준비되다 reports the state: 준비됐어요? = ready? — the doorway word, the waiter's, the exam proctor's. Answer with M9's 다: 다 준비됐어요.

en: to be read; to read easily (also: make someone read)
notes: M2's 읽다 + 히 — one of the guests the M36 md said to 'recognize them and nod' at ('읽히다 (get read)'); today it takes a seat. 잘 읽히는 책 (badge from M24) = a book that reads easily; 이 글은 잘 안 읽혀요 (M32's 글) = this text doesn't read well. Double agent — the M37 md: '읽히다, 씻기다 — same shape, both parties' — so 아이한테 책을 읽히다 = make the child read. Sound: 읽혀요 says 일켜요 — the buried ㄹ that M2's 읽다 note said 'comes back before a vowel' returns, and the ㄱ fuses with ㅎ into ㅋ.

en: to be eaten; to get through, work
notes: M1's 먹다 + 히 (the 히-row of the M36 table: 먹다 → 먹히다), the guest the M36 md filed as 'get eaten — the food chain's verb': 작은 물고기는 큰 물고기한테 먹혀요 (M22's 물고기). Its daily job is the idiom: 말이 안 먹혀요 (M4's 말) = my words don't get eaten = they don't get through; 잘 먹히다 = it works, it lands, it sells — a joke, a pitch, a product. Says 머키다: ㄱ and ㅎ fuse.

en: to be mixed, get mixed up
notes: M40's 섞다 ('colors, cards, playlists, and languages all get 섞다-ed') + 이, the shape of the 이-row in the M36 table (보이다, 놓이다, 쓰이다): things mix on their own. 물과 기름은 안 섞여요 (M1's 물, M40's 기름) = water and oil don't mix — the science-class sentence and the personality one; 여러 언어가 섞여 있어요 (M29's 여러, M26's 언어) = several languages are mixed in; 감정이 섞이다 (M42's 감정) = feelings get mixed. The ㄲ carries over: 섞여요 says 서껴요.

en: to take (clothes, a peel) off someone or something
